rationale: A wins because it knows where the facts stop. Its line, "The acquisition and the enterprise AI tool are supplied as separate facts. The connection is plausible and unconfirmed," is exactly the adult supervision this announcement needs. B has punchier packaging, but "220 million users already inside companies" takes a supplied user number and smuggles in a workplace-adoption claim. That is how a decent pitch gets a reporter to ask, "Says who?"
gaps_in_A: "The launch is today, and it is the first product move that can be read against those two numbers" overclaims sequence; the update does not say this is Canva's first enterprise-relevant product move.
"Why IT admins should care about Canva's single sign-on" is dismissed too quickly as `duplicate`; IT/admin tooling could become its own trade angle if Canva has IT-buyer proof.
The set is strong but still missing a sharper warning that without named enterprise customers, even the best Adobe/Microsoft fight risks being company positioning, not market evidence.
gaps_in_B: "220 million users already inside companies" is not in the update. Monthly users are not the same thing as workplace penetration.
"Notion, Figma, and Miro ran the same arc" and "Canva is the largest consumer-originated design tool to attempt it" are outside facts presented as context without sourcing.
"so the legal team can make a slide deck without asking design" invents a user, workflow, and artifact. Cute line, bad discipline.

"Adobe has positioned Firefly with similar 'on-brand, generative, safe for commercial use' language" may be true in the world, but it is not grounded in the supplied update. The set keeps reaching for facts it was not given.
